Rites
rīts
n. pl. (prescribed acts of worship; rendering Hebrew mishpat, the appointed manner)
Latin ritus, a religious usage. The Authorized Version has the word once, beside ceremonies, in the law of the passover.

Biblical Definition

A rite is an appointed act of worship, done in a prescribed manner. “In the fourteenth day of this month, at even, ye shall keep it in his appointed season: according to all the rites of it, and according to all the ceremonies thereof, shall ye keep it” (Num 9:3). The insistence on manner runs through the Law: Nadab and Abihu offered “strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not” and died (Lev 10:1–2); Uzzah steadied the ark and was struck, because the ark was to be borne on the shoulders of Levites (2Sa 6:6–7). Under the new covenant the Lord left two: baptism (Mat 28:19) and the Supper — “this do in remembrance of me” (Luk 22:19).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines rite as the manner of performing divine or solemn service, as established by law, precept, or custom; a formal act of religion or other solemn duty.

RITE, n. The manner of performing divine or solemn service, as established by law, precept or custom; a formal act of religion or other solemn duty. Rites are ceremonies of religion.

Key Scripture

Num 9:3 — "In the fourteenth day of this month, at even, ye shall keep it in his appointed season: according to all the rites of it, and according to all the ceremonies thereof, shall ye keep it."

Lev 10:1 — "And Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, took either of them his censer, and put fire therein, and put incense thereon, and offered strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not."

Lev 10:2 — "And there went out fire from the LORD, and devoured them, and they died before the LORD."

Mat 28:19 — "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:"

Luk 22:19 — "And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me."

Modern Corruption

The manner of worship is treated as a matter of taste, and the two men who improvised at the altar were carried out in their coats.

expand to see more

Leviticus 10 is the shortest argument for the regulative principle in Scripture. Nadab and Abihu were priests, at the altar, offering incense to the true God, on the day of their consecration; the fire they used was one He commanded them not, and it killed them. The offence is defined by absence, not by prohibition — there was no verse forbidding that fire, and there did not need to be. Aaron held his peace. The Reformed conclusion is that in worship what God has not appointed He has not authorised, and the burden of proof lies on the innovation rather than on the objector.

Modern worship is largely governed by the opposite rule: whatever is not forbidden is permitted, and the question asked of a new practice is whether it works. That is the normative principle, and it is held sincerely by good men; but it is not the principle of Leviticus 10, and its results are visible. A congregation that has no test but effect will in time worship in whatever manner the age finds effective, and the manner will teach a doctrine that the pulpit has not examined.

The counter-corruption is a Reformed vice: to hold the regulative principle so tightly that the two ordinances Christ actually left are administered thinly and infrequently, while the energy goes into policing what others do. Numbers 9:3 is a command to keep the passover, and to keep it exactly; the exactness serves the keeping. A church that guards the manner and neglects the ordinance has the argument and not the meal.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mishpat (H4941), the appointed manner, ordinance; chuqqah (H2708), statute; Greek esh zarah is the Hebrew for strange fire, zar (H2114), foreign, unauthorised.

expand to see more

Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — ordinance, prescribed manner, rite; Numbers 9:3, 9:14, Exodus 26:30.

Hebrew zar (H2114) — strange, unauthorised; Leviticus 10:1, Numbers 3:4, 26:61.

Greek anamnesis (G364) — remembrance; Luke 22:19, 1 Corinthians 11:24–25.

Usage

"“According to all the rites of it” — the manner commanded with the meal."

"“Which he commanded them not” — the offence defined by absence."

"“This do in remembrance of me” — one of the two the Lord left."
